title: Who wrote the March 1926 session songs; Herschel's endings
summary: She sorts out which songs were hers and which Clarence Blair's, how Louis played behind any song, and how Herschel's ending became "Mighty Tight Woman".

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Well, two days, a couple days after that big O.K. night in March, 1926, you did record with Louie behind you and the tunes were 'A Jealous-Woman Like Me,' --
And then a couple of days later, you did 'The Mailtrain Blues,' --
-- and 'A Man For Every Day in the Week.'
Yeah, 'A Man Every Day in the Week.' Uh-huh.
Now, I'd like to ask you if you could -- could you try to think about those sessions and remember those sessions and --
Well, those songs didn't belong to me.
Those didn't belong to me. Those were Clarence Blair's (PHONETIC) numbers.

Blair made "Mailtrain." "Jealous Woman" was mine and "Special Delivery" was mine. "Jack of Diamonds" was mine. "Jealous Woman Like Me" is mine, because I was so jealous. I was so jealous, let me tell you, --
Is that why you wrote that song?
Well, now, when -- of course, your brother Herschel, he was playing the piano, he knew the songs.
So how did he learn the songs?
Well, he -- a trumpet can play behind any song because they just play the ending of a song, you know?
So he didn't have to learn the songs. He just listened.
So after he played the -- see, Herschel, I made that song ________ ending. "Herschel, you sure have

Every song that Herschel played, he used to always play a beautiful ending. So I said, "Herschel, that's such a pretty ending, I believe I'll make me a song out of that." He said, "All right." He said, (Singing). I say, "I come to you sweet man and I'm falling on my knees (singing)." That's where I start off, "I'm a Mighty Tight Woman."
I got such a bad cold, my nose is stopped up.
